summary: Prasenjit Sarkar opens by describing the industry shift from traditional IDE-based coding (VS Code, JetBrains, Cursor) to agentic platforms (Codex, Claude, Devin, Gemini CLI), citing a Pragmatic Engineer Survey from March 2026 showing 55% of developers regularly use AI agents. He questions whether LLM-generated code is trustworthy, maintainable, and secure. Sonar created an evaluation framework that ran 4,444 distinct open-source Java programming assignments through 53+ models, analyzed with SonarQube Enterprise. Unlike standard benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, SWE-bench) that measure functional correctness, Sonar's framework also captures security issues, reliability, engineering discipline, and technical debt. Performance results show significant variation: Gemini 3.1 Pro High achieved an 84.17% SWE-bench pass rate with 307,000 lines and moderate issue density. Claude Sonnet 4.6 generated 627,000 lines with the highest security issue rate at 300 per million lines. GPT 5.4 Pro High generated 1.2 million lines—massive code bloat. GPT-4o generated under 250,000 lines. Sarkar attributes LLM code quality problems to mixed-quality training data, built-in security flaws, hidden subtle logic errors, the probabilistic nature of LLMs, limited context understanding, and lack of explainability. He notes newer models produce finer, harder-to-detect bugs even as overall vulnerability counts decrease. The Sonar LLM Leaderboard at sonar.com/leaderboard publicly publishes these evaluations. Two complexity metrics are discussed: cyclomatic complexity (counting branches/loops) and cognitive complexity (Sonar proprietary, measuring human readability difficulty). Sarkar introduces the ACDC framework with three stages: Guide (Sonar Context Augmentation and Sonar Sweep in private beta), Verify (SonarQube Agentic Analysis in open beta, running in 1-5 seconds before commit versus 1-5 minutes in CI), and Solve (SonarQube Remediation Agent for issues that slip through to PRs). The remediation agent creates one PR per issue, runs each fix through analysis and compilation to check for regressions, and discards fixes that introduce problems—ensuring no regression-causing code is presented. It can also be invoked from the SonarQube dashboard to address accumulated tech debt, with developers reviewing and merging approved fixes. Sonar's product portfolio spans Guide, Verify, and Solve across 40+ programming languages and frameworks, with IDE partnerships, DevOps support, and marketplace presence.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Sonar evaluated 53+ LLM models against 4,444 Java programming assignments using SonarQube Enterprise, publishing results on a public leaderboard.
Standard benchmarks like SWE-bench measure functional correctness but miss security, maintainability, and engineering quality dimensions.
GPT 5.4 Pro High generated 1.2 million lines—extreme code bloat—while GPT-4o generated under 250,000 lines for the same assignments.
Claude Sonnet 4.6 had the highest security issue rate at 300 per million lines of code among evaluated models.
LLM code quality issues stem from mixed-quality training data, built-in security flaws, hidden logic errors, probabilistic generation, limited context, and lack of explainability.
The ACDC framework (Guide, Verify, Solve) integrates SonarQube analysis into agentic workflows, catching issues in 1-5 seconds before commit.
The remediation agent creates one PR per issue, validates each fix through analysis and compilation, and discards fixes that would cause regressions.
The remediation agent can also be invoked from the SonarQube dashboard to batch-fix accumulated technical debt, with developer review before merge.
Sonar's product portfolio spans 40+ programming languages and frameworks with IDE, DevOps, and marketplace integration.

sections.title: Introduction and the Shift to Agentic Development
sections.summary: Sarkar introduces the topic of LLM-generated code quality and describes the industry shift from IDE-based coding to agentic platforms, citing a Pragmatic Engineer Survey showing 55% of developers regularly use AI agents.

sections.title: Evaluating LLM Code Quality and Reliability
sections.summary: Contrasts standard LLM benchmark pass rates (80%+) measuring functional correctness with missing dimensions: security, real-world reliability, engineering architecture, maintainability, and technical debt.

sections.title: Sonar's Evaluation Framework and Methodology
sections.summary: Describes Sonar's evaluation framework running 4,444 distinct open-source Java programming assignments through models, analyzed with SonarQube Enterprise to generate critical insights for LLM selection.

sections.title: LLM Performance Analysis (Pass Rates and Code Bloat)
sections.summary: Presents specific model results: Gemini 3.1 Pro High at 84.17% pass rate with 307K lines, Claude Sonnet 4.6 with 627K lines and highest security issue rate (300/million), and GPT 5.4 with 1.2M lines, highlighting significant code bloat in newer models.

sections.title: Why LLMs Struggle: Training Data and Hidden Flaws
sections.summary: Explains root causes of LLM code quality issues: mixed-quality training data, built-in security flaws, hidden logic errors, probabilistic nature, limited context, and lack of explainability.

sections.title: The Sonar LLM Leaderboard
sections.summary: Introduces sonar.com/leaderboard with 53+ evaluated models, open-sourced data, and detailed per-model breakdowns. Gemini 3.1 Pro High leads with 84.17% correctness; five models exceed 80% accuracy.

sections.title: Complexity Metrics: Cyclomatic vs. Cognitive
sections.summary: Defines cyclomatic complexity (branch/loop count) and cognitive complexity (Sonar proprietary, measuring human readability difficulty). Notes newer models generate more code with higher complexity and finer bugs.

sections.title: The ACDC Framework: Guide, Verify, and Solve
sections.summary: Introduces ACDC with three stages: Guide (Sonar Context Augmentation and Sonar Sweep in private beta), Verify (SonarQube Agentic Analysis in open beta, 1-5 second pre-commit analysis via MCP), and Solve (SonarQube Remediation Agent for PR-stage issues).

sections.title: Remediation Agent Details and Product Portfolio
sections.summary: Details the remediation agent's verify loop: creating one PR per issue, running each fix through analysis and compilation, discarding regression-causing code. Also covers batch tech-debt remediation from the SonarQube dashboard. Concludes with product portfolio spanning 40+ languages and frameworks, IDE partnerships, DevOps support, and marketplace presence.

demonstrations: Sonar LLM Leaderboard at sonar.com/leaderboard showing pass rates, lines of code, cyclomatic complexity, cognitive complexity, bugs, and security issues per model.
SonarQube Agentic Analysis integrating with agentic coding platforms (Claude, Codex, Gemini CLI) via MCP for pre-commit analysis.
SonarQube Remediation Agent creating one fix per issue, running each through analysis and compilation, discarding regression-causing fixes.
SonarQube dashboard tech-debt remediation: selecting all issues and assigning them to the agent for batch PR creation.
limitations: Standard LLM benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, SWE-bench) only measure functional correctness on known test cases, missing security, reliability, and engineering quality.
LLMs are probabilistic—same prompt to same model on different days may produce different code.
LLMs have limited context understanding of company data, codebase, and architecture.
LLM-generated code is not explainable, making diagnosis and improvement difficult.
Training data contains mixed quality code with built-in security flaws and hidden subtle logic errors.
Newer models produce finer bugs that are very hard for humans to detect.
